_comment: Domain knowledge that no general-purpose embedding model carries.
An advisor asking for 'address proof' wants the electricity bill, but nothing in the bill's
text is distributionally close to that phrase: it talks about meter readings and direct
debits. Five embedding models were measured on this corpus (all-MiniLM-L6-v2,
multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1, msmarco-MiniLM-L6-cos-v5, e5-small-v2, bge-small-en-v1.5) and all
five ranked the bill 13th or worse for that query while ranking every other probe first.
The association is procedural knowledge about which documents evidence what, so it is supplied
explicitly here rather than hoped for from the model.
A query reaches a rule by meaning, not by containing one of its phrases: each rule's paraphrases and
its concept name are embedded once at startup with the model the semantic arm searches with, and a
query fires the rule when its vector comes within search.concept-floor of one of them and within
search.concept-floor-ratio of the best rule's score — the second number is what stops 'proof of
address' dragging 'evidence of identity' in. So 'documents that show where the client lives' reaches
the address rule though none of its words appear here. Paraphrases are examples, not a list to
complete: state the requirement the way an advisor would, avoid words every client query carries
('client' on its own pulls unrelated queries towards a rule) and acronyms ('photo ID' became the
nearest phrasing for reference codes and nonsense), add one when a real query shows up in the search
log with concepts=[] and should not have, then run ConceptFloorTest and read its table — a phrasing
close to another rule's wording narrows the margin between them.
Each rule's expansions are the documents a UK firm may rely on for that requirement, and their order
is a budget: a query naming one concept runs the first four, a query naming two runs two of each, so a
fifth would never run, and a probe that reaches nothing in the seeded corpus (payslip, council tax
bill, deputy appointed by the court) sits after the ones that do — it is there for a corpus that holds
one, and a two-concept query never spends a slot on it. QueryExpanderTest prints what each probe
reaches; docs/search-design.md, 'Where the lexicon comes from', has the table.
Sources, read in their current text. Address: JMLSG Guidance Part I (June 2023, revised August 2025)
5.3.75 — 'Current council tax demand letter, or statement' and a document from 'a regulated utility
company' — and 5.3.76 — 'current bank statements, or credit/debit card statements, issued by a
regulated financial sector firm in the UK, or utility bills'. Identity: 5.3.75's photographic list —
'Valid passport', 'Valid photocard driving licence (full or provisional)', 'National Identity card' —
and 5.3.90's control of 'requiring copy documents to be certified by an appropriate person'. Income:
FCA MCOB 11.6.13G(1) 'Examples of evidence of income ... are payslips and bank statements' and
11.6.9G(2) 'checking the level of income regularly paid into a bank account'. Capacity: Mental Capacity
Act 2005 s.9, under which a lasting power of attorney confers authority only once 'registered in
accordance with Schedule 1', and s.16(2)(b), the court-appointed 'deputy'. Source of funds and wealth:
JMLSG 5.5.32 — 'a copy of the relevant will' where wealth comes from inheritance, 'evidence of
conveyancing' where it comes from the sale of property.
Named by the texts and measured out: 'tax return' (MCOB 11.6.9G(5)) put five documents that merely
mention self-assessment on the income page; every wording of 'pension statement' (11.6.15G(2)) scored
the suitability report on pension consolidation above the benefit statement it was meant to reach
(0.61–0.68 against 0.50–0.52). 'mortgage statement' is on the seeded firm's own accepted list and not
in JMLSG; it cost 'address proof' a rank (4 to 5) for a document the sparse arm already finds.
'tenancy agreement' is named by neither, and its only reach here was the tenants' address, not the
client's.
These lists are configuration, not something a model could learn, because the texts set a standard
and leave the list to the firm. JMLSG 5.3.112 says the guidance 'does not require that in all cases a
customer's address should be verified', and Part I sets no numeric recency for an identity or address
document — only 'current' and 'recent' — where the seeded onboarding checklist wants one 'dated within
the last three months'; that checklist refuses the mobile phone bill which Onfido's proof-of-address
list (18 of the 78 document types in its public API specification) accepts, and takes a national
identity card 'issued by an EEA state' only, a restriction 5.3.77 allows. Two firms reading the same
text produce two lists; this file holds one firm's.
'life cover paid on death' shipped in the first version and was removed: no text makes life cover an
evidentiary requirement, the policy schedule is the top result for its phrasings on meaning alone
(0.55 for 'death benefit'), and its probes only raised the relative floor — 'policy written in trust
beneficiaries' at 0.67 pulled the trust deed and the estate-planning notes onto the page while cutting
the pension statement that also states a death benefit.
Expansions widen the semantic arm only. The lexical arm exists to match exact tokens, and OR-ing
extra terms into it would cost precision for recall the semantic arm already provides; the sparse arm
was measured with the probes and without and they changed no rank, only page length.

paraphrases: something that shows where the client lives
something that confirms the client's home address
a way to prove who someone is
how a person proves their identity
confirming that a person is who they say they are
proof of what the client earns
expansions: salary credit on a bank statement

rules.concept: acting for someone who has lost capacity
paraphrases: who can act for someone who can no longer manage their own affairs
someone appointed to make decisions for a person who has lost capacity
expansions: lasting power of attorney attorney appointed

rules.concept: source of funds and source of wealth
paraphrases: where did the money come from
how the money being invested was acquired
expansions: proceeds from the sale of a property
